findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The newly added block calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but this module has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (see the import list at lines 1-20). This is a TypeScript compile error and, at runtime, a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` that will be thrown on every `getClient()` call, i.e. on every Salesforce event create/update/delete. The Salesforce app is completely broken by this change.

findings.title: Google Calendar credential key is overwritten with the zod safeParse wrapper object
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)`, i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, not the parsed data. Here `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` is passed straight into `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, so after the first token refresh the stored credential key becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` instead of the token object. `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will then fail for that credential forever, breaking Google Calendar for every user whose token refreshes. Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the data). Either return `.data` from the helper or use `key.data` here.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the refreshed token response has no `refresh_token`, the helper sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers merge this data into the stored credential, e.g. office365calendar does `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` and persists it, and zoomvideo does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`. Providers that legitimately omit `refresh_token` on refresh (Microsoft, and any provider in credential-sync mode) will therefore have their valid stored refresh token overwritten with the garbage value `"refresh_token"`, permanently breaking the integration for that user. The old code kept the previous refresh token because the field was optional.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys are a no-op and expiry is never validated
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` do not create dynamic keys: `toString()` on a Zod schema yields `"[object Object]"`, so the object literal ends up being `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() }` (the second computed key overwrites the first). The documented intent ("assume that any property with a number is the expiry") is not implemented, so in credential-sharing mode nothing but `access_token` is validated. Concretely, zoomvideo then computes `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` with `expires_in` undefined → `NaN`, and because `isTokenValid` compares `NaN < Date.now()` (false), the adapter will keep returning the stale access token and never refresh again.

findings.title: Credential-sync branch returns a raw fetch Response while callers expect provider-specific shapes
findings.body: In the sync branch the helper returns the `Response` object from `fetch(CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT)`, but the non-sync branch returns whatever the provider client returns, and callers rely on those shapes: googlecalendar reads `res?.data` (gaxios response), zoho-bigin and zohocrm read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token` (axios response), hubspot casts the result directly to `HubspotToken` and reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn`, and larkcalendar passes it to `handleLarkError` expecting `{code, data}`. With credential sharing enabled these paths will throw `TypeError`s or persist nonsense (e.g. hubspot writes a `Response` object as the credential key and an `NaN` expiryDate). The helper should normalise the sync response into the same shape each caller expects, and should also check `response.ok` before returning.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects a userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Passing the credential's primary key means the self-hosted endpoint is asked for the tokens of an unrelated user id (credential ids and user ids are different sequences), so the wrong user's access token can be fetched and stored on this credential, leaking access to a third party's Bigin account. `refreshAccessToken` must receive and forward `credential.userId`.

findings.title: appStoreMetadata is keyed by app directory name, not slug, so most apps resolve to 404
findings.body: `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` assumes the metadata map is keyed by slug, but `@calcom/app-store/appStoreMetaData` is keyed by the app's directory name (e.g. `googlecalendar`, `office365calendar`, `zoomvideo`), which differs from the DB slug (`google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `zoom`). For every app whose dirName != slug the lookup returns `undefined` and the webhook responds 404 "App not found. Ensure that you have the correct app slug", making credential sync unusable for exactly the apps this PR wires up. Look the app up by iterating the metadata values and matching `slug`, or select `dirName` from the `app` row.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes the token on every call but then connects with the old access token
findings.body: `getClient()` now unconditionally POSTs a `refresh_token` grant to Salesforce on every instantiation (i.e. for every createEvent/updateEvent/deleteEvent), ignoring whether the stored token is still valid, and then builds the `jsforce.Connection` with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` — the *old* token from the credential — instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. So the refresh achieves nothing for the current request while adding a network round trip and burning Salesforce refresh-grant rate limits on every booking operation. Gate the refresh on expiry and use the newly obtained access token/instance URL for the connection.

findings.title: Zoom passes "zoomvideo" as the app slug to the sync endpoint
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug (and the `appId` stored on the credential, see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts` which creates `{ appId: "zoom" }`) is `zoom`. A self-hoster's sync endpoint keyed on the Cal.com app slug will not recognise `zoomvideo`, so Zoom token sync silently fails or returns the wrong app's credentials. The slug argument should match the app slug used everywhere else (`zoom`).

findings.title: Unvalidated input paths throw unhandled exceptions (500 + stack traces)
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt(...)` (line 57) and `JSON.parse(...)` (line 57) all throw on malformed input, and nothing wraps them in try/catch, so a bad body, a wrong encryption key, or non-JSON plaintext produces an unhandled rejection and a generic 500 instead of a 400 with a useful message. There is also no HTTP method check, so a plain GET to this route (no body) hits the same crash path. Use `safeParse`, wrap the decrypt/parse in try/catch, and reject non-POST requests.

findings.title: findFirst ignores users with multiple credentials for the same app
findings.body: A user can legitimately have several credentials for one app (e.g. two Google Calendar accounts, multiple Zoom accounts). `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks an arbitrary one and overwrites its `key` with the synced tokens, silently corrupting the other account's credential (its calendar/video calls will then act on the wrong external account) and never creating a second credential when one is genuinely needed. The payload has no way to identify which credential is meant; consider including an external account identifier or the credential id in the webhook payload.

findings.title: Synced credential update does not clear the `invalid` flag
findings.body: When a credential was previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. Google Calendar's `invalid_grant` handling, or `invalidateCredential` in the Zoom/Webex adapters), the update at lines 73-80 only writes `key`. The credential stays flagged invalid, so Cal.com keeps showing the app as broken and keeps skipping it even though fresh, working tokens were just synced in. The update should also set `invalid: false`.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED evaluates to the encryption key string instead of a boolean
findings.body: `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` returns the value of `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` when both are set, so this exported "flag" actually holds a secret. Any place that logs, serialises, or returns this constant (it is a general-purpose constants module imported widely) would disclose the credential encryption key. Wrap it in `!!(...)` so the exported value is a boolean.

findings.title: Webex wraps refreshOAuthTokens but still validates with the strict provider schema
findings.body: The refresh call now goes through `refreshOAuthTokens` (so it can hit the credential-sync endpoint), but the response is still validated with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse`, which requires `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in` and a literal `scope`/`token_type`. The sync endpoint is documented in `refreshOAuthTokens` to return "only the access token and expiry date", so in credential-sharing mode this parse always fails and the refresh rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — Webex can never be synced. Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` here as the other adapters do, or don't route Webex through the sync helper.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh uses statusText equality and a hardcoded login host
findings.body: `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` is an unreliable success check: fetch implementations return an empty `statusText` for HTTP/2 responses, which would make a successful refresh throw `HttpError` with an empty message. Use `!response.ok` instead. Additionally the token endpoint is hardcoded to `https://login.salesforce.com`, which fails for sandbox/My Domain orgs (`test.salesforce.com` / instance URL); the stored `credentialKey.instance_url` or a configurable host should be used.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality
findings.body: The shared secret check uses `!==` on the raw header value. For a secret-equality check on an unauthenticated endpoint, a constant-time comparison (`crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers) is preferable to avoid leaking information about the secret through response timing. Also note the header lookup relies on the configured name being lowercase (Node lowercases incoming header keys); normalising with `.toLowerCase()` would avoid a silent 403 if a self-hoster configures `Calcom-Webhook-Secret`.

findings.title: Outlook token-refresh error diagnostics were removed
findings.body: The previous code logged the zod error and the raw Microsoft response when the refresh response failed validation. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` now throws a generic `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` with no provider payload, and the surrounding code no longer logs anything, making Outlook refresh failures (a common support issue) effectively undebuggable. Include the validation error / response body in the thrown error or log it before throwing.

findings.title: No tests for the new credential-sync webhook or the token-parsing helpers
findings.body: This PR adds a new unauthenticated-by-default HTTP endpoint that writes third-party OAuth credentials into the database, plus two shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) that every OAuth app now depends on, with no unit or integration tests. Given the bugs reachable in these code paths (wrong metadata key lookup, safeParse wrapper persisted as a credential key, `refresh_token` defaulting to a literal string), tests covering secret rejection, disabled-feature rejection, create vs. update behaviour, and the sync/non-sync branches of the helpers should accompany the change.
